    Significance test for the bias-adjusted undirected PIT-Wasserstein metric

    u_pit_significance.Rd

    Tests the weakest of the three null hypotheses in the PIT-Wasserstein family: that the predictive distributions have the right shape given an arbitrary location error. The bias adjustment absorbs any common shift, so a rejection here means the shape of the predictive distribution is wrong — skew, tail weight, or a mixture of dispersion errors — and not that the forecasts are merely off-centre. One-sided, as U_pit is a distance.

    u_pit_significance(U_pit, n_predictions)

    Arguments

    U_pit

    the bias-adjusted undirected PIT-Wasserstein metric, as returned by pit_w() or prediction_scores()

    n_predictions

    the number of predictions each U_pit was computed from, as returned by prediction_scores()

    Value

    a dataframe with one row per input value and columns:

    • U_pit, n_predictions — as supplied

    • statistic — \(\sqrt{n}\,U_{pit}\), the quantity with a fixed null

    • expected — the null mean of U_pit

    • critical_0.05 — the one-sided 5% critical value of U_pit

    • p_value — the probability of a U_pit at least this large under the location-free null

    Details

    Because the adjustment estimates a parameter from the same data, the null is not the baseline \(\int_0^1|B^\circ|\) of b_pit_significance(): it is the bridge with the estimated direction projected out (see .u_pit_null), giving a 5% critical value about 0.66 times the baseline one at every n. Using the baseline null here would be badly conservative. The adjusted null is still distribution-free — it depends on n and nothing else — but has no published c.d.f., so it is simulated once per session and cached.

    U_pit says nothing about the direction of a dispersion error; pair it with d_pit_significance(), which does.

    Unit tests

    

# the adjusted null is strictly tighter than the baseline one
testthat::expect_lt(
  u_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05,
  b_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05
)

# the critical value scales as 1/sqrt(n)
testthat::expect_equal(
  u_pit_significance(0, 400)$critical_0.05 * 2,
  u_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05,
  tolerance = 1e-6
)

# a statistic at the null mean is not significant
testthat::expect_gt(u_pit_significance(u_pit_significance(0, 100)$expected, 100)$p_value, 0.3)

# the 5% critical value returns a p value of about 0.05
crit = u_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05
testthat::expect_equal(u_pit_significance(crit, 100)$p_value, 0.05, tolerance = 0.005)

# vectorised over both arguments
testthat::expect_equal(nrow(u_pit_significance(c(0.02, 0.09), c(76, 76))), 2L)
